Check yourself

1. Your electron temperature is 120 mK and your Zeeman energy is 64 µeV. By how much would you need to raise the magnetic field to recover EZ = 15 kBTe? What would that cost?

Show answer
kBT at 120 mK is 10.3 µeV, so 15 kBT is 155 µeV, about 2.4 times the present Zeeman energy. The total field would have to go from 0.55 T to about 1.3 T, and the qubit frequency from 15.4 GHz to about 37 GHz. Microwave delivery at 37 GHz is much harder, heating grows, T1 typically shortens strongly at higher field, and the micromagnet gradients do not scale up. Lowering Te is almost always the better choice.

2. A line has 20 dB at 4 K and nothing else. What noise temperature reaches the device, and why is that a problem for a 15 GHz qubit?

Show answer
T = 300/100 + 4 × 0.99 ≈ 7 K. At 15.4 GHz, hf/kB ≈ 0.74 K, so the thermal photon number is 1/(e0.74/7 − 1) ≈ 9. That noise can drive spin transitions, heat the electrons, and add dephasing. Further attenuation on the colder stages is needed.

3. Why is a directional coupler placed at the mixing chamber instead of at room temperature?

Show answer
If the incoming and reflected waves were separated at room temperature, the reflected signal would have to travel back up through all the attenuators on the input line, losing tens of decibels before reaching any amplifier. With a cold coupler, the reflected signal goes straight into a low-loss output line and the 4 K amplifier, preserving its signal-to-noise ratio.
PreviousChapter 3 · From chip to sample holderNextChapter 5 · The electronics around the fridge

Part B · Getting a chip ready and cold · Chapter 5

The electronics around the fridge

Outside the fridge sits a rack of instruments, each solving one problem: holding gate voltages steady, measuring tiny currents, playing fast pulses, generating microwaves, and reading out the sensor. This chapter explains what each instrument does for our device, why each needs the specifications it has, and how they are tied together in time. The exact brands vary from lab to lab; the jobs do not.

5.1The jobs to be done

Our device needs six kinds of signal. It is worth listing them before looking at any hardware, because the requirements follow directly from the physics:

JobWhere it goesWhat it needsWhy
Static gate voltagesevery gatemany channels, µV stability, high resolution, slow safe rampsThey set the electrostatic landscape. Their noise moves the dots directly.
Transport and DC sensingohmic contactspA–nA current measurement, small AC excitationFirst characterization; current through the sensor
Fast gate pulsesP1, P2, B2 (via bias tees)ns timing, mV amplitudes, long sequences, triggersMoving between initialization, manipulation and readout; exchange pulses
Microwave burstsP1 (MW)10–20 GHz, phase control, shaped envelopesEDSR rotations of each qubit
Readout carrier and demodulationsensor ohmic O3 (tank)stable ~200 MHz tone, low-noise amplification, fast demodulationSingle-shot charge detection in microseconds
Timing and synchronizationall instrumentsa common clock and a master triggerEvery pulse and every measurement must line up

5.2Static gate voltages

Every gate needs a DC voltage that stays put, often for days. The instrument is a multichannel low-noise DC source, essentially a rack of precision digital-to-analog converters with filtered outputs: 24 to 48 channels with 18 to 25 bits of resolution, a few volts of range, and very low noise. Commercial units used widely in the field include QDevil's QDAC and Basel Precision Instruments' LNHR DAC, and many groups build their own [30].

Three properties matter most:

  • Noise. A fluctuating gate voltage is indistinguishable from charge noise: it moves the dot levels. At a lever arm of 0.1 eV/V, 10 µV of noise on a plunger moves the dot by 1 µeV. Good sources are quiet at the microvolt level, and the fridge filters remove what remains above a few kilohertz.
  • Resolution. You need to place a dot level to a fraction of the thermal energy, which means steps of well under a millivolt. A room-temperature voltage divider (for example 1:5 or 1:10) is often added on sensitive gates: it reduces the range and the noise and improves the resolution by the same factor.
  • Safe ramping. Gates are fragile. The software layer enforces maximum voltages for every gate and ramps between values slowly, so that a mistyped "5" instead of "0.5" does not destroy a device.
Worked numbers: resolution in energy

A 20-bit source spanning ±10 V has steps of 20 V / 2²⁰ ≈ 19 µV. Through a 1:10 divider that becomes 1.9 µV at the gate, or 0.19 µeV at a lever arm of 0.1 eV/V: far finer than anything we need.

A 14-bit pulse generator spanning ±1 V has steps of 2 V / 2¹⁴ ≈ 122 µV. After 10 dB of line attenuation (a voltage factor of 0.32), that is 39 µV at the gate, about 3.9 µeV of dot energy. That is close to the thermal energy, which is coarse for a readout level. This is why fast generators are used for changes around an operating point set precisely by the DC source, not for setting the operating point itself.

5.3Measuring currents: transport and DC sensing

The first measurements on a cold device are transport measurements: a small bias across two ohmics, and a measurement of the current that flows through the device. The currents are tiny, from picoamperes to nanoamperes, so the current is converted to a voltage by a transimpedance amplifier (also called a current preamplifier) with a gain of 10⁷ to 10⁹ V/A. High gain means low noise but low bandwidth, typically a kilohertz or so at the highest gains.

Most transport is measured with a lock-in amplifier. A small AC excitation, typically 10 to 100 µV at a low frequency such as 77 Hz (chosen to avoid harmonics of the mains frequency), is added to the source–drain bias. The lock-in multiplies the resulting current by a reference at the same frequency and averages, recovering only the part of the current that responds to the excitation: the differential conductance dI/dV. This rejects offsets, drifts and most of the 1/f noise of the amplifier. The excitation must be small compared with kBTe/e (about 4 µV at 50 mK) to probe the true linear response, or at least small compared with the features you want to resolve. For first surveys, larger excitations are acceptable.

A variation used for charge sensing is to apply a small square wave to a gate instead of the bias, and lock in to the sensor current at that frequency. This measures the transconductance dI/dVgate, which highlights charge transitions as sharp lines. HRL used exactly this to map their first undoped dots [8].

5.4Fast pulses

An arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) plays pre-programmed voltage waveforms on several channels with nanosecond timing. For spin qubits it must provide:

  • enough amplitude: after line attenuation, pulses of 1 to 50 mV at the plunger and barrier gates;
  • sample rates around 1 GS/s or more, so edges and exchange pulses can be shaped at the nanosecond level;
  • long sequences built from reusable segments, since a single experiment may contain thousands of different pulse sequences;
  • marker and trigger outputs, to start other instruments at the right moment.

The AWG's outputs are usually DC-coupled, so a waveform can hold a level for milliseconds; the bias tee on the sample board then defines the lowest frequency that actually reaches the gate (Chapter 3). Modern "qubit controllers", from companies such as Zurich Instruments, Qblox, Quantum Machines and Keysight, or open-source designs built on RFSoC FPGA boards, combine AWG channels, microwave generation, digitizers and a real-time sequencer in one system. That makes feedback and conditional operations much easier [6, 30].

5.5Microwave drive

EDSR needs bursts at the qubit frequencies, 15.42 and 15.72 GHz for our device, with precisely controlled duration, amplitude and phase. The phase matters because it defines the rotation axis: a burst with phase 0 rotates about x, one with phase 90° about y (Chapter 19). The standard way to make such bursts is IQ modulation:

  • A microwave source provides a continuous local oscillator (LO) tone, say at 15.50 GHz.
  • An AWG provides two baseband waveforms, I(t) and Q(t), oscillating at an intermediate frequency (IF) of tens to a few hundred megahertz and shaped by the pulse envelope.
  • An IQ mixer multiplies them together to produce a burst at LO ± IF. The sign is chosen by the relative phase of I and Q. With IF = −80 MHz the output is at 15.42 GHz (qubit 1); with IF = +220 MHz it is at 15.72 GHz (qubit 2). One LO and one mixer can thus drive both qubits.

Real mixers are imperfect. Some LO leaks through, and an unwanted mirror-image sideband appears at LO ∓ IF. Both must be calibrated away with small DC offsets and amplitude and phase corrections on I and Q. An uncorrected sideband at the wrong frequency can drive the other qubit. Many labs use vector signal generators that contain the mixer and its calibration. The key point is that phase coherence comes from the LO: as long as the LO runs continuously and the IF waveforms are timed on a fixed clock, every burst has a well-defined phase relative to the qubit's rotating frame.

5.6Readout electronics

For reflectometry (Chapter 10), a stable RF source generates the carrier near the tank's resonance frequency, around 205 MHz for our device. It is sent down the attenuated input line, and the reflected wave comes back through the HEMT amplifier. At room temperature the signal is amplified further and then demodulated: multiplied by a copy of the carrier and its 90°-shifted version, and low-pass filtered. The result is the in-phase and quadrature components I and Q of the reflected signal. A charge transition changes the tank's impedance, which shifts the reflected signal by a small vector in the IQ plane.

Demodulation can be done with analog mixers followed by a digitizer, or entirely digitally by sampling the RF signal directly and multiplying in an FPGA, as lock-in amplifiers and qubit controllers do. Digital demodulation also makes it easy to integrate over a chosen window and compare the result with a threshold in real time, so the controller knows within microseconds whether the sensor saw a charge transition. That is what real-time feedback, such as initialization by measurement, requires [6].

5.7Timing and synchronization

Every instrument that generates or measures a time-dependent signal contains its own clock. Left alone, the clocks drift apart by parts per million, and a 15 GHz drive would slip in phase relative to the AWG's IF waveforms. Two measures keep everything coherent:

  • A common frequency reference. One instrument (or a dedicated rubidium or crystal reference) distributes a 10 MHz reference signal to all the others, and each locks its internal clocks to it. All frequencies in the system are then fixed multiples of one master clock.
  • A master trigger. One sequencer starts each repetition of the experiment and triggers the others: the AWG starts its pulses, the microwave burst is gated, the digitizer starts recording. The timing between them is calibrated once, including cable delays, and then stays fixed.

With these in place, timing jitter between instruments is in the picosecond range, which is irrelevant for spin qubits: a jitter of 10 ps on a 125 ns π pulse changes the rotation angle by less than 10⁻⁴. What does matter is that the phase of every microwave burst is referenced to the same continuously running LO, and that the software tracks the phase of each qubit's rotating frame through the sequence (Chapter 22).

5.8Software

The software stack is as much a part of the experiment as the hardware. In most groups it has four layers:

  1. Instrument drivers that talk to each box over Ethernet, USB or GPIB.
  2. A gate layer that knows each gate's safe limits and ramp rates, and implements virtual gates (Chapter 11), so you can ask for "move dot 1's level by 50 µeV" and the software adjusts several physical gates together.
  3. A measurement framework that runs sweeps, builds pulse sequences, stores data with all instrument settings, and plots results. Common open-source choices are QCoDeS, Quantify and the QICK/spinQICK packages; many groups use their own.
  4. A calibration manager that stores the current best values of every calibrated parameter (the device passport, in effect) and the routines that update them [6].

Two habits pay for themselves many times over. Save every instrument setting with every dataset, automatically. Six weeks later, nobody remembers which divider was on P2. And keep the device passport in the software, not just in a notebook, so that every experiment reads the same calibrated values.

5.9The signal map of our device

Putting it together, Figure 5.1 shows what is connected to what for our device.

Lab notebook · first day cold

Base 10 mK reached 06:20. All instruments on common 10 MHz (from rubidium reference); trigger master = AWG marker 1.

Gate limits loaded: plungers/barriers −0.2 V … +1.0 V, lead gates −0.2 … +1.5 V, CS −0.5 … +0.3 V; ramp 10 mV/s. Dividers 1:5 on P1, P2, SP.

Lock-in: 77.7 Hz, 100 µV excitation on O1 (transport), current amp 10⁸ V/A on O2. Ready to un-ground lines one by one.

Check yourself

1. Why not simply set the readout level of a plunger with the AWG, instead of combining a DC source with AWG pulses?

Show answer
The AWG's resolution and stability are coarser. A 14-bit generator over ±1 V has 122 µV steps, which after the line becomes several µeV of dot energy, comparable to the thermal energy. A precision DC source sets the operating point with sub-µeV resolution and low drift; the AWG only adds relative pulses on top.

2. An IQ mixer is driven with LO = 15.50 GHz and IF = −80 MHz, and its image sideband is poorly suppressed. At what frequency is the image, and why could that matter for our device?

Show answer
The wanted output is at LO + IF = 15.42 GHz, and the image is at LO − IF = 15.58 GHz. That is not on qubit 2 (15.72 GHz), but it is only 140 MHz away, and a strong image or other spurious tones can still drive off-resonant rotations or heat the device. With other IF choices the image could land right on the other qubit, so IF frequencies are chosen with this in mind and the sideband is calibrated away.

3. Two instruments are not locked to a common reference and their clocks differ by 1 ppm. How much phase does a 15 GHz drive slip relative to the AWG over 100 µs?

Show answer
A 1 ppm error at 15 GHz is 15 kHz. Over 100 µs that accumulates 15 kHz × 100 µs = 1.5 cycles, about 540° of phase. Without a common reference, the rotation axes of successive pulses would be essentially random over a Ramsey or echo sequence.
PreviousChapter 4 · The fridge as part of the experimentNextChapter 6 · Waking the device up: leakage, turn-on and ohmics

Part C · First signs of life · Chapter 6

Waking the device up: leakage, turn-on and ohmics

The first hours at base temperature answer simple questions with big consequences. Does every gate hold voltage without leaking? Do the ohmic contacts reach the quantum well? At what voltage do electrons first appear? A device that fails here cannot be rescued by clever tuning, so these checks come first, and they are done slowly and carefully, one line at a time.

6.1First, do no harm

The device has been sitting with every line grounded at the breakout box. Before anything is released, the software limits are loaded (Chapter 5), every DC channel is set to 0 V, and the instruments are connected. Lines are then un-grounded one at a time. Each gate is ramped slowly, at around 10 mV/s, never stepped. A step of a volt applied in microseconds charges the gate capacitance with a current pulse, and through the stray capacitance between layers it can put an unintended voltage across thin oxide. A slow ramp makes the same change harmless.

It is also worth deciding in advance how far each gate will be allowed to go. In our device the plungers and barriers should never need more than about +1 V, and the lead gates perhaps +1.5 V. The limits sit a little above that, so that a typing error is caught by software rather than by the device.

6.2Leakage: does each gate hold its voltage?

A gate is a capacitor plate. Once charged, it should draw no steady current. If it does, current is flowing through the oxide into the semiconductor or into another gate, a gate leak. Leakage is checked for every gate individually: ramp it from 0 V towards its maximum while all other gates stay at 0 V, and record the current it draws. Many DC sources can measure their own output current. Otherwise a sensitive ammeter in series, or a large series resistor with a voltmeter across it, does the job.

Two other currents are worth watching during the same sweep: the current on the other gates, which reveals gate-to-gate shorts, and the current on the ohmic contacts, which reveals leakage into the quantum well. With the lead gates at 0 V there is no electron gas, so any current reaching an ohmic must have come through an oxide.

What counts as acceptable? A healthy gate draws no current above the instrument's noise floor (tens of picoamperes at most) over its whole planned range. A gate that leaks only above some voltage, like the one in Figure 6.1, is usable as long as it stays well below that onset. Its limit is lowered in the software and noted in the passport. A gate that leaks at a few hundred millivolts is effectively dead, and any gate shorted to another will behave as part of that other gate.

When it goes wrong

What you see: raising gate B2 makes a current appear on gate P1, proportional to the B2 voltage.

Likely cause: a resistive short between B2 and P1 through the oxide separating their layers, which would show up as a resistance of perhaps megaohms between the two lines.

What to do: measure the resistance between the two lines directly. If it is high (gigaohms), the effect may be capacitive pickup during the ramp, which disappears when the ramp stops. If it is resistive, the two gates must be operated with small voltage differences, or one of them sacrificed. Record it in the passport so that nobody later "discovers" it again.

6.3Turning on: making electrons appear

Our heterostructure contains no electrons until a gate pulls them in (Chapter 2). The first real measurement is therefore the turn-on: the gate voltage at which a conducting channel first forms between two ohmic contacts.

The procedure is simple. Apply a small AC excitation between two ohmics, say 100 µV at 77 Hz on O1, and measure the current at O2 with a lock-in. Then sweep all the gates along the path between them together: the lead gates LL and LR, and the plungers and barriers in the channel. Because every gate on the path rises together, the only question being asked is "is there any electron gas at all?". The screening gates stay near 0 V so that they define the channel.

The result looks like the left panel of Figure 6.1. Below threshold, nothing. At threshold, the conduction band under the gates dips below the Fermi level of the ohmics, and electrons flow in. Above threshold, the electron density grows roughly linearly with gate voltage, and so does the conductance, until the series resistance of the ohmic contacts and the filters limits the current.

Several things can be read from this one curve:

  • The threshold voltage (0.36 V here) tells you where the device's electrostatics starts. Dots will form at somewhat higher voltages on the plungers, and barriers will pinch off near this value (Chapter 7).
  • The saturation level tells you the total series resistance. With 100 µV excitation and about 10 nA at the top of our sweep, the resistance is about 10 kΩ. That includes the ohmic contacts, the filters (a few kilohms in our fridge, Chapter 3) and the channel itself. A curve that saturates at a much lower current suggests a poor ohmic contact.
  • Hysteresis, the difference between up- and down-sweeps, comes from charges that become trapped at the interface or in the oxide when the gate is raised, and are released only slowly. A small hysteresis of tens of millivolts, as here, is normal. A large one (hundreds of millivolts), or a threshold that keeps moving from sweep to sweep, warns of an unstable device that will be hard to tune.
  • Noise and jumps just above threshold come from the electron gas being so dilute that it percolates through disorder. A smooth turn-on suggests a clean interface. Large, irregular jumps suggest charge traps nearby.

Industrial-scale characterization uses exactly this measurement to compare devices across a wafer. Intel, for example, reported turn-on and related statistics across hundreds of devices on 300 mm wafers [31].

Worked numbers: what density do we have?

The electron gas under a gate behaves like one plate of a parallel-plate capacitor, with the gate as the other plate. The capacitance per area is ε/d, where d is the distance from the gate to the well and ε the permittivity of the material in between.

For 30 nm of SiGe (relative permittivity about 13) plus about 10 nm of Al₂O₃ (about 9), the series combination gives C/A ≈ ε₀ / (30 nm/13 + 10 nm/9) ≈ 8.85 × 10⁻¹² / (3.4 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻³ F/m².

Each additional volt above threshold then adds a density n = (C/A)·ΔV/e ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻³ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.6 × 10¹⁶ m⁻², which is 1.6 × 10¹² cm⁻² per volt. At 0.3 V above threshold the density is around 5 × 10¹¹ cm⁻², typical for the reservoirs of Si/SiGe qubit devices [8].

6.4Testing every ohmic

With the channel on, each ohmic contact is checked in turn. Measure the two-terminal resistance between pairs of ohmics through the accumulated channel. If O1–O2 conducts, O1–O3 does not, and O2–O3 does not, then O3 (or its bond, or its line) is the problem. The sensor channel is checked the same way: accumulate SL, SR, SP and the sensor barriers together, and measure O3 to O4. Its turn-on voltage will be similar to the qubit channel's, but not identical, because the sensor channel sits under a slightly different gate geometry.

A contact that does not conduct at all might be an open bond or line (check its continuity from the breakout box), an ohmic implant that misses the well, or a lead gate that does not reach over the ohmic. The first can sometimes be fixed in the next cooldown. The others are fabrication problems.

6.5For comparison: waking up a GaAs device

A modulation-doped GaAs device starts the other way round. Its electron gas is already present at zero gate voltage, so the ohmics conduct as soon as the device is cold, and two-terminal resistances of a few kilohms are normal. The first gate tests are then depletion tests: each gate is made negative until the electrons beneath it are pushed away and the current through the channel falls (Chapter 7). Leakage checks are similar, but at negative voltages. Above a certain negative voltage on a Schottky gate on GaAs, current starts to tunnel through the barrier.

When it goes wrong

What you see: no current at any gate voltage, even well above the expected threshold.

Possible causes: the excitation is not reaching the device (check the lock-in output and the line); an ohmic or its bond is open; one gate on the path does not turn on (broken gate, so the channel stays depleted under it); or a wrong polarity convention in the software.

What to do: confirm continuity from the breakout box. Try a different pair of ohmics. Then sweep the gates on the path one at a time with all others high: the one whose sweep makes no difference is probably disconnected.

Lab notebook · day 1, afternoon

Leakage, each gate alone up to its limit: all < 20 pA. B3 starts leaking at 1.55 V → limit lowered to 1.2 V. No gate-to-gate shorts found.

Global turn-on O1→O2 (LL, LR, P1, P2, B1–B3 together, CS = 0): threshold 0.36 V up, 0.335 V down. 10 nA at 0.8 V with 100 µV → ≈ 10 kΩ total. Small jumps near threshold, otherwise smooth.

Sensor channel O3→O4: turn-on 0.39 V, similar shape. All four ohmics fine. Parked: all channel gates at 0.6 V, CS at 0 V.

Check yourself

1. Why are all the gates along the path swept together for the first turn-on, instead of one at a time?

Show answer
Current can only flow if electrons are accumulated under every gate along the path. Sweeping one gate alone while the others stay at 0 V would show nothing, because the others keep the channel empty. Sweeping them together tests the simplest possible question, whether a channel forms at all, and finds the overall threshold. Individual gates are then tested by lowering them one at a time from the "all open" state (Chapter 7).

2. A turn-on curve shows 300 mV of hysteresis, and the threshold moves by 50 mV every time you repeat the sweep. What does this suggest, and how would you proceed?

Show answer
Many charge traps near the interface or in the oxide are being filled and emptied as the gates move, so the electrostatic landscape is not stable. Tuning will be frustrating, because every large excursion changes the device. A common strategy is to sweep once to a working point, then avoid large excursions and let the device settle; some groups find it helps to wait or to cycle the gates a few times. If the instability persists, it may be better to switch to another device on the chip.

3. Using the capacitance estimate in the worked example, how much does the reservoir density change if the lead gate is raised by 50 mV?

Show answer
About 1.6 × 10¹² cm⁻² per volt × 0.05 V = 8 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻². That is a 16% change on a density of 5 × 10¹¹ cm⁻², which is why lead gates are usually set once and left alone: changing them changes the reservoirs, and with them the tunnel barriers next to them.
PreviousChapter 5 · The electronics around the fridgeNextChapter 7 · Pinch-offs, barriers and the first dot

Part C · First signs of life · Chapter 7

Pinch-offs, barriers and the first dot

Once the channel conducts, every gate is tested individually: lowering it should close the channel beneath it. The voltages at which gates "pinch off", and the way they do it, form a map of the device's electrostatics. Two barriers set just below pinch-off, with a plunger between them, make the first quantum dot, and its Coulomb peaks are the first truly quantum signal from the device.

7.1One gate at a time

Start from the "all open" state of Chapter 6: every gate along the O1–O2 path at 0.6 V, comfortably above threshold, with a small AC bias and a lock-in measuring the current. Now lower one gate while keeping all the others fixed. As long as there is still an electron gas under it, current flows. When the gate falls below the local threshold, the electrons beneath it are pushed out, a potential barrier rises across the channel, and the current stops. That gate has pinched off the channel.

A pinch-off curve tells you more than one number:

  • Does the gate work at all? A gate whose tip is disconnected from its pad cannot pinch off, so its curve stays flat no matter how far you lower it. This is the first test that catches broken gates (Chapter 3).
  • Where does it pinch off? The voltage, relative to the turn-on threshold, tells you how strongly the gate couples to the well. Gates in higher layers are farther from the well and usually need larger swings.
  • How sharply? The width of the transition reflects the gate's lever arm on the barrier. A very gradual pinch-off suggests weak control. A very abrupt one suggests a strong gate, which will need finer steps later.
  • What happens near zero? Bumps and resonances just before pinch-off come from tunnelling through small, unintended puddles of electrons trapped by disorder. A few are normal. Many large, irregular resonances warn that the potential under the gate is rough.

Plungers are tested the same way. Lowering a plunger also pinches off the channel, since the dots must sit under accumulated electrons too. Knowing every gate's pinch-off gives you a starting point for every gate when you build a dot.

In GaAs, the equivalent experiment is done with negative voltages on depletion gates, and a narrow constriction between two gates (a quantum point contact) shows something beautiful as it pinches off: its conductance falls in steps of 2e²/h, the conductance quantum, as one-dimensional channels close one by one [1]. The steep edge of the last step makes a quantum point contact an excellent charge sensor. Such plateaus are seldom clean in silicon devices, where disorder, the heavier effective mass and the valley degree of freedom blur them, so silicon devices usually use sensor dots instead (Chapter 9).

7.2Two barriers make a dot

A quantum dot needs a region of electrons separated from the reservoirs by two tunnel barriers. In our device, dot 1 sits under P1, bounded by B1 on the left and B2 on the right. Set P1 to a moderate value and map the current through the device as a function of both barrier voltages at once (Figure 7.2).

This map is the classic way to find a dot. Far from the corner, the barriers are either fully open (no isolated region, just a channel) or fully closed (no current at all). In the corner, both barriers are high enough to isolate the region between them, but thin enough that electrons can still tunnel through. Then Coulomb blockade appears: current flows only when the energy of the dot lines up with the reservoirs, which happens at a discrete set of gate voltages.

The diagonal direction of the resonances is itself informative. Raising either barrier lowers the potential in the dot slightly (each barrier has a lever arm on the dot as well as on its tunnel barrier), so a resonance condition is met along lines where the sum of the two effects is constant. A resonance line that runs along a different direction, or that responds to only one barrier, belongs to a different, unintended dot, often one formed by disorder under a single gate.

Once peaks are found, the barriers are set a little inside the corner: closed enough that the peaks are sharp, open enough that the peak current is easy to measure. From then on the barriers stay fixed, and the plunger does the counting.

7.3The constant-interaction picture

To interpret Coulomb peaks quantitatively, the field uses a simple model: the constant-interaction model [32, 1]. It treats the dot as a small conductor with a total capacitance CΣ to its surroundings, of which Cg is to the plunger gate. The energy needed to add the N-th electron, the dot's electrochemical potential, is

\[ \mu(N) = \left(N - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)E_C - e\,\alpha\, V_g + E_N + \text{const}, \qquad E_C = \frac{e^2}{C_\Sigma},\quad \alpha = \frac{C_g}{C_\Sigma}. \]

Here EC is the charging energy, α is the lever arm of the gate, and EN is the single-particle (orbital) energy of the level the N-th electron occupies. An electron can tunnel onto the dot from the source and off to the drain only when μ(N) lies between the source and drain electrochemical potentials. At near-zero bias that happens only at isolated plunger voltages, which are the Coulomb peaks.

The spacing between consecutive peaks follows directly. Moving from μ(N) = 0 to μ(N + 1) = 0 requires

\[ \Delta V_g = \frac{E_C + \Delta E}{e\,\alpha}, \]

where ΔE = EN+1 − EN is zero when the two electrons share an orbital (spin up and spin down) and equal to the orbital or valley spacing otherwise. Without ΔE this reduces to ΔVg = e/Cg: the plunger must add exactly one electron's worth of induced charge.

Worked numbers: peak spacing for our device

With EC = 6.5 meV and α = 0.10 eV/V, two peaks that share an orbital are separated by ΔV = 6.5 meV / (0.10 eV/V) = 65 mV on the plunger.

A peak that requires an extra orbital of 3 meV is separated by (6.5 + 3) / 0.10 = 95 mV.

A many-electron dot, which is larger and therefore has a smaller charging energy of perhaps 2 meV, shows peaks about 20 mV apart. As the dot empties, the spacing grows. That growth is the first sign that you are approaching the last electrons (Chapter 11).

7.4How each gate acts on the dot

The plunger is not the only gate that moves the dot. Every nearby gate has some capacitance to it, and that cross-coupling becomes important as soon as there are two dots. It is measured directly from the peaks. Map the current versus the plunger and one other gate X. Each Coulomb peak appears as a line, and its slope tells you the relative strength of the two gates:

\[ \left.\frac{dV_P}{dV_X}\right|_{\text{peak}} = -\frac{\alpha_X}{\alpha_P}. \]

A steep line (X has little effect) means weak cross-coupling, a shallow one strong cross-coupling. In our device, B1 and B2 each have about 30% of P1's lever arm on dot 1, and P2 about 30% as well. These ratios will become the off-diagonal elements of the virtual-gate matrix in Chapter 11.

7.5A dot is not yet a qubit dot

The first dot you find is usually a many-electron dot, tens of electrons in a puddle larger than intended, because the gates are still well above the voltages needed for few electrons. That is fine. It is the right object for the next two chapters: measuring the lever arm and charging energy with Coulomb diamonds, measuring the electron temperature, and forming a charge sensor. Reducing the qubit dots to one electron each comes later, once the sensor can count electrons where transport current no longer can (Chapter 11).

When it goes wrong

What you see: in the barrier–barrier map, there are resonances, but they respond to only one barrier, or run at odd angles, or there are many overlapping sets of them.

Likely cause: unintended dots formed by disorder, typically under one of the barriers, or a double dot where you expected a single dot.

What to do: raise the plunger to deepen the intended dot, which makes it dominate. Try a different region of the map. Check whether the stray resonances move with a gate that should not influence them, which tells you where they are. Sometimes a different combination of barrier settings, or the neighbouring dot, behaves much better.

Lab notebook · day 2

Pinch-offs (others at 0.6 V): B1 0.18 V, B2 0.26 V, B3 0.21 V; P1 0.30 V, P2 0.31 V; SB1 0.22 V, SB2 0.24 V. All gates pinch off, so all tips are connected.

B1 vs B2 map at P1 = 0.50 V, P2 = 0.6 V (P2 region used as part of the right lead): clean diagonal Coulomb peaks below B1 ≈ 0.28, B2 ≈ 0.35. Parked at B1 = 0.24, B2 = 0.31.

P1 sweep: regular peaks every ≈ 21 mV → many-electron dot (E_C ≈ 2 meV if α ≈ 0.1). Next: Coulomb diamonds for the lever arm.

Check yourself

1. A barrier's pinch-off curve stays flat at the open-channel conductance down to −0.2 V. What does that tell you?

Show answer
The gate has no effect on the channel, which almost always means its tip is electrically disconnected from its bond pad (a break in the gate line), or the wrong line is being swept. Check the line assignment and bond map first; if they are right, the gate is broken.

2. In a map of current versus P1 and B1, a Coulomb peak line has a slope dVP1/dVB1 = −0.3. What is B1's lever arm on dot 1 if P1's is 0.10 eV/V?

Show answer
αB1/αP1 = 0.3, so αB1 = 0.03 eV/V. Raising B1 by 10 mV lowers the dot by 300 µeV, equivalent to raising P1 by 3 mV.

3. Why do the Coulomb peaks in the barrier–barrier map of Figure 7.2 run along diagonals?

Show answer
Both barriers have lever arms on the dot's potential as well as on their own tunnel barriers. Raising either one lowers the dot level, so the resonance condition μ(N) = 0 is met along lines where the combined effect of the two barriers is constant, i.e. lines with negative slope. A resonance that ignores one of the barriers is probably a different, unintended dot.
PreviousChapter 6 · Waking the device up: leakage, turn-on and ohmicsNextChapter 8 · Coulomb diamonds, lever arms and electron temperature

Part C · First signs of life · Chapter 8

Coulomb diamonds, lever arms and electron temperature

Gate voltages are what you control, but energies are what matter. The measurement that converts one into the other is bias spectroscopy, which produces the diamond-shaped patterns that appear in almost every quantum-dot thesis. From one diamond plot you get the lever arm, the charging energy and the orbital spacing. From the width of a single Coulomb peak you then get the electron temperature. Every later chapter uses these numbers.

8.1Bias spectroscopy

In Chapter 7, Coulomb peaks were measured with almost no bias across the dot: a peak appears only when the dot's electrochemical potential μ(N) lines up exactly with the Fermi level of the reservoirs. Now apply a finite source–drain bias VSD. The source and drain Fermi levels separate by eVSD, opening a bias window, and current flows whenever some μ(N) lies inside that window. Sweep the plunger and the bias together, plot the differential conductance dI/dVSD, and the regions of blockade appear as diamonds (Figure 8.1).

The geometry of a diamond follows from requiring μ(N) to sit at the edge of the bias window. Inside a diamond, μ(N) is below both reservoirs and μ(N+1) is above both, so the electron number is fixed. The diamond closes at a bias equal to the energy needed to add one more electron, the addition energy Eadd = EC + ΔE. Its width along the gate axis, at zero bias, is the peak spacing of Chapter 7, Eadd/(eα). Dividing height by width gives the lever arm directly:

\[ \alpha = \frac{V_{SD}^{\text{tip}}}{\Delta V_g}, \]

where VSDtip is the bias at the diamond's tip and ΔVg its width at zero bias. An equivalent method uses the slopes mS and mD of the two edges of a diamond, which works even when the diamond is not symmetric because the bias is applied to only one side [11]:

\[ \alpha = \left|\frac{m_S\, m_D}{m_S - m_D}\right|. \]
Worked numbers: reading Figure 8.1

The N = 1 diamond spans P1 = 450 to 515 mV, so ΔVg = 65 mV, and closes at VSD ≈ 6.5 mV. The lever arm is α = 6.5/65 = 0.10, i.e. 0.10 eV/V or 100 µeV per mV.

The addition energy for the second electron is Eadd = eVSDtip = 6.5 meV. Since the first two electrons share the lowest orbital (spin up and spin down), this is the charging energy.

The excited-state line meets the diamond edge at a bias of 3 mV, so the first excited orbital lies 3 meV above the ground state. Our dot is small and steep: comparable values have been reported in overlapping-gate Si/SiGe devices [7].

8.2Excited states, shells and valleys

The faint lines inside the conducting regions are not a nuisance; they are spectroscopy. When the bias window is wide enough to include an excited state of the dot as well as the ground state, a second transport channel opens and the current steps up. The bias at which the step appears gives the excitation energy directly. In our device the first excited orbital is 3 meV up, far above anything else that matters, which is exactly what a qubit dot should have.

Following the addition energy from one electron number to the next reveals the dot's shell structure. In a silicon dot, each orbital can hold four electrons: two spins times two valley states. If the valley splitting is large, the addition energies show a small bump after two electrons (the lower valley full) and a larger one after four (the whole orbital shell full). Princeton saw exactly such a bump at the 4 → 5 transition in all nine dots of their array [7]. Valley splittings of a few hundred µeV are small compared with charging energies, though, so diamonds rarely measure them precisely. Chapter 14 uses better methods.

8.3Is the dot really empty?

The diamond to the left of the first transition in Figure 8.1 never closes. That is what an empty dot looks like: there is no further electron to remove, so no further transition bounds the blockade. It is tempting to conclude from transport alone that the dot is empty, and in very clean devices, transport can indeed be followed down to the last electron [7]. But there is a trap. As the dot empties, it also shrinks, its tunnel barriers grow thicker, and the current through it can fall below the measurement noise even though electrons remain. Peaks that simply disappear are not proof of N = 0. Proof comes from a charge sensor, which sees an electron leave the dot whether or not any current flows through it (Chapters 9 and 11).

8.4Electron temperature from a Coulomb peak

A Coulomb peak has a finite width because the reservoirs' Fermi distributions do. When the tunnel coupling is weak enough that the level's lifetime broadening hΓ is much smaller than kBTe, the peak shape is set purely by temperature [33]:

\[ G(V_g) \propto \cosh^{-2}\!\left(\frac{e\,\alpha\,(V_g - V_0)}{2\,k_B T_e}\right), \qquad \text{FWHM} = 3.53\,\frac{k_B T_e}{e\,\alpha}. \]

The lever arm enters because the peak is measured in gate voltage but broadened in energy. This is one reason it is measured first.

Worked numbers: what width to expect

At Te = 50 mK, kBTe = 4.3 µeV. With α = 0.10 eV/V the FWHM is 3.53 × 4.3 µeV / 0.10 eV/V ≈ 152 µV, about 0.15 mV on the plunger.

At 200 mK the peak would be 0.61 mV wide. If you see 0.6 mV wide peaks at base temperature, your electrons are at about 200 mK, and Chapter 4's checklist applies.

Three conditions must be satisfied for the width to mean temperature, and each is a classic source of error:

  1. Lifetime broadening must be negligible. If the barriers are too open, the peak gets an extra Lorentzian width hΓ. Close the barriers until the width stops decreasing; only then is the width thermal.
  2. The excitation must be small. An AC excitation comparable to kBTe/e (about 4 µV here) broadens the peak itself. Use a few microvolts, or measure at zero bias with a charge sensor.
  3. The measurement must not heat what it measures. A sensor excitation that is too large warms the reservoirs. Princeton found Te rising steadily once their sensor excitation exceeded about 85 µV peak to peak [27].

The most reliable version of this measurement, used once a charge sensor works, watches the occupation of a qubit dot as its level is swept through the reservoir's Fermi level. The time-averaged occupation then traces out the Fermi function directly, with no transport through the dot at all. Princeton found 120 mK this way in an early device [7], and later 45 mK after improving thermalization [27].

8.5The sensor dot gets the same treatment

The sensor channel's dot is characterized in exactly the same way: a barrier–barrier map to form it, diamonds to measure its lever arm and charging energy. Our sensor dot is larger than the qubit dots, by design. That gives it a smaller charging energy (about 4 meV), a smaller lever arm from its plunger (about 0.08 eV/V), and broad, strongly conducting peaks, which make a good sensor (Chapter 9).

When it goes wrong

What you see: the diamonds do not close cleanly. Their edges are broken into segments, or extra diamonds of different sizes overlap.

Likely cause: more than one dot in series, often a disorder dot under a barrier in addition to the intended one. Two dots in series produce a pattern of overlapping or irregular diamonds instead of a regular chain.

What to do: return to the barrier–barrier map (Chapter 7) and find settings where only one set of resonances appears, typically by opening the suspect barrier slightly.

Check yourself

1. A diamond is 40 mV wide in plunger voltage and closes at 2.4 mV of bias. What are the lever arm and the addition energy?

Show answer
α = 2.4/40 = 0.06 eV/V, and Eadd = 2.4 meV.

2. A Coulomb peak measured with α = 0.06 eV/V has a FWHM of 0.5 mV. What electron temperature does that imply, assuming thermal broadening? What would you check before believing it?

Show answer
kBTe = FWHM × eα / 3.53 = 0.5 mV × 0.06 / 3.53 ≈ 8.5 µeV, so Te ≈ 99 mK. Before believing it, check that the width does not shrink when the barriers are closed further (no lifetime broadening), that the excitation is a few µV or less, and that the width follows the fridge temperature when the fridge is heated.

3. Why is the disappearance of Coulomb peaks in transport not sufficient proof that a dot is empty?

Show answer
As the dot empties and shrinks, its tunnel barriers become thicker and the current through each remaining peak falls exponentially. Peaks can drop below the measurement noise while electrons are still in the dot. A charge sensor detects the electron number directly, regardless of whether current can flow through the dot.
PreviousChapter 7 · Pinch-offs, barriers and the first dotNextChapter 9 · A charge sensor: counting electrons without current

Part C · First signs of life · Chapter 9

A charge sensor: counting electrons without current

Transport stops working exactly where things get interesting: when the qubit dots hold only one or two electrons, almost no current can flow through them. From here on, every measurement goes through a charge sensor, a separate dot whose current responds to the charges nearby. This chapter forms the sensor, chooses its operating point, and shows what it can and cannot do when read out with an ordinary DC current measurement.

9.1How a sensor sees a single electron

The sensor dot SD sits about 100 nm from dot 2. The two are not tunnel-coupled; no electron can hop between them. But they are capacitively coupled: an electron arriving in dot 2 raises the electrostatic potential at the sensor slightly, which shifts the sensor's levels up, exactly as if its plunger SP had been lowered a little. If the sensor is tuned onto the steep side of one of its Coulomb peaks, that small shift becomes a large change in its conductance [34, 1].

The size of the shift, expressed as an equivalent voltage on the sensor's plunger, is approximately

\[ \Delta V_{SP} \approx \frac{e\,C_m}{C_{SP}\,C_{\Sigma,2}}, \]

where Cm is the mutual capacitance between dot 2 and the sensor, CSP is the capacitance between the sensor dot and its plunger, and CΣ,2 is the total capacitance of dot 2 [7]. The shift falls off steeply with distance, because in a densely gated device the metal overhead screens the field of the electron (Chapter 2). In our device one electron in dot 2 shifts the sensor peak by about 0.16 mV of SP-equivalent voltage, a sizeable fraction of the peak's width. An electron in dot 1, farther away, shifts it by less, about 0.10 mV.

9.2Choosing the operating point

The sensor's job is to turn a small potential shift into the largest possible change in signal, so it is parked where the slope of its peak is steepest (Figure 9.1). A few practical considerations refine that choice:

  • Peak height and width. A tall, broad peak gives a larger current and therefore a better signal-to-noise ratio, as long as the shift per electron is still a reasonable fraction of the width. That is why the sensor dot is made larger than the qubit dots and its barriers are set fairly open: its peaks are lifetime-broadened and strongly conducting (around 0.5 e²/h), not sharp and thermally limited.
  • Dynamic range. A sensor on the steepest flank responds linearly only for shifts much smaller than the peak width. Several electrons moving at once, or a slow drift, push it off the flank, and the response becomes non-linear or even changes sign.
  • Which side? Either flank works, but they respond with opposite signs. Pick one and stay on it, so that "the sensor signal went up" always means the same thing.

Princeton reported sensor shifts of about 0.26 mV per electron for the nearest dot in their nine-dot array, and HRL typical maximum fractional current changes of 20% [7, 8]. Our numbers are similar.

9.3Keeping the sensor on its flank

The moment you start sweeping the qubit dots' gates to look for their charge transitions, a problem appears. P2 is about 100 nm from the sensor dot, so it has a small direct capacitance to the sensor, too. Sweeping P2 by 100 mV moves the sensor's level as much as several millivolts on SP would, which drags the sensor through its own Coulomb peaks. The resulting signal is a large sawtooth from the sensor itself, with the small steps from dot 2's charge transitions buried in it (Figure 9.2, orange).

The cure is compensation. Measure how much SP must change to undo a given change in P2, the ratio of P2's lever arm on the sensor to SP's, and let the software adjust SP automatically whenever P2 moves. HRL did exactly this with linear corrections to the sensor plunger, which held the sensor's sensitivity constant over large gate sweeps for hours [8]. With compensation, the sensor stays on its flank, and only real charge transitions change the signal (Figure 9.2, blue). This is the simplest example of a virtual gate (Chapter 11).

9.4The limit of DC sensing: speed

So far the sensor current has been measured the ordinary way: a small bias across the sensor, and a room-temperature current amplifier at the end of a long cable. This works well for mapping charge transitions slowly. But spin readout needs to catch a single electron tunnelling, often within microseconds, and here DC sensing runs into a hard limit.

The sensor is a resistor of 50 to 100 kΩ on the steep flank of its peak. The cable from the device to the room-temperature amplifier, with its filters, has a capacitance to ground of roughly a nanofarad. Together they form an RC low-pass filter.

Worked numbers: why DC sensing is slow

With R = 100 kΩ and C = 1 nF, the time constant is RC = 10⁵ × 10⁻⁹ = 100 µs, and the bandwidth 1/(2πRC) ≈ 1.6 kHz.

A tunnelling event that lasts 50 µs, typical of spin readout, is washed out completely.

The fridge filters, designed to keep the electrons cold (Chapter 4), make it worse. In practice a DC-measured sensor in a well-filtered fridge reaches a few kilohertz to a few tens of kilohertz. Princeton, for example, filtered a 500 kHz-sampled DC sensor signal to 30 kHz, the bandwidth of their amplifier [7].

There are two ways out. One is to put the current-to-voltage conversion close to the device: Princeton later used a 20 kΩ resistor on the sample holder with cryogenic amplifiers at 1 K and 4 K, reaching about 1 MHz bandwidth [27], and HRL uses a similar cold transimpedance arrangement [35]. The other, and the most widely used, is radio-frequency reflectometry, which sidesteps the cable capacitance by making it part of a resonant circuit (Chapter 10).

9.5Watching electrons tunnel in real time

Even with a few kilohertz of bandwidth, the sensor can do something remarkable: watch a single electron hop on and off a dot in real time. Tune dot 2's level close to the Fermi level of its reservoir, and close its barrier B3 until the electron tunnels at, say, 100 Hz. The sensor signal then switches randomly between two levels, one for N electrons and one for N + 1. This is a random telegraph signal.

Two numbers come out of such a trace. A histogram of the signal shows two peaks, and the ratio of their separation to their width is the sensor's signal-to-noise ratio at that bandwidth. Princeton measured SNR = 6.9 at 30 kHz [7]. From the SNR and the bandwidth B follows the charge sensitivity, δq ≈ e/(SNR·√B), which for Princeton's numbers is 8 × 10⁻⁴ e/√Hz. The second number is the time-averaged occupation as the dot's level is swept slowly through the Fermi level. It traces out the reservoir's Fermi function, and its width gives the electron temperature with no transport through the dot at all (Chapter 8).

9.6What the sensor shows first

With a compensated sensor, sweeping P1 and P2 shows charge transitions that are completely invisible in transport, right down to the last electron. The next step is to make those sweeps fast enough to explore large regions of gate space, and to understand the pattern of lines that two dots produce. That needs a faster sensor, which is the subject of the next chapter. The pattern itself, the charge stability diagram, is the subject of Chapter 11.

When it goes wrong

What you see: the sensor signal occasionally jumps by a large amount and stays there, or its sensitivity changes from hour to hour.

Likely cause: a charge trap near the sensor switching state. That shifts the sensor peak by a fraction of its width, exactly like a real electron would. Slow drift of the gate voltages or of trapped charges has a similar, gradual effect.

What to do: re-centre the sensor on its flank regularly. Groups automate this: before each measurement, a short sweep of SP finds the steepest point again. If one trap switches often, try a different sensor peak or a slightly different sensor configuration, which can move the sensor away from the trap.

Check yourself

1. Why is the sensor dot deliberately made larger, and its barriers more open, than the qubit dots?

Show answer
A sensor needs a large current and a steep, but not too narrow, Coulomb peak, so that a small potential shift gives a large, linear change in current with good signal-to-noise ratio. A larger dot with open barriers has broader, strongly conducting peaks. The qubit dots need the opposite: small size, large charging and orbital energies, and weak, controlled tunnelling.

2. A sensor shows SNR = 4 at a bandwidth of 10 kHz. What is its charge sensitivity, and what SNR would you expect at 100 kHz if the noise is white?

Show answer
δq ≈ e/(4 × √10⁴) = e/400 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ e/√Hz. With white noise, the noise amplitude grows as √B, so at 100 kHz the SNR falls by √10 to about 1.3, too low for reliable single-shot detection.

3. In our device, P2's cross-coupling to the sensor is 0.012 V/V, and the sensor peak is about 0.56 mV wide (FWHM) on SP. How far does an uncompensated 200 mV sweep of P2 move the sensor, and what happens to the measurement?

Show answer
The sensor moves by 0.012 × 200 mV = 2.4 mV of SP-equivalent voltage, about four peak widths. Starting on one flank, it is dragged across the top of its peak, down the other flank and into Coulomb blockade, where it no longer responds to anything. Transitions in the first part of the sweep appear as small kinks on a large background, and those in the last part are invisible. Compensating SP keeps it on the flank throughout.

Part D · Seeing single electrons fast · Chapter 10

RF reflectometry from the ground up

The DC sensor of Chapter 9 sees single electrons, but only a few thousand times per second, because the cable's capacitance shorts out its signal. Radio-frequency reflectometry turns that same capacitance into part of a resonant circuit and measures the sensor's resistance through the reflection of a weak radio wave. It brings the readout from milliseconds down to microseconds, and it is how nearly every modern spin-qubit experiment reads its sensor [5, 36, 37].

10.1The idea: measure a resistance by reflection

Send a radio-frequency wave down a 50 Ω cable towards a load. If the load's impedance Z equals the cable's impedance Z₀, the wave is absorbed completely. If not, part of it is reflected, with a complex reflection coefficient

\[ \Gamma = \frac{Z - Z_0}{Z + Z_0}. \]

The sensor dot is the load, but it is a poor one: its resistance on the flank of a peak is 50 to 100 kΩ, thousands of times larger than 50 Ω. Attached directly to the cable, it reflects almost everything whether its resistance is 50 kΩ or 100 kΩ, so Γ barely changes and nothing can be measured. The solution is an impedance-matching network that transforms the sensor's large resistance down to about 50 Ω. Then small changes of the sensor's resistance produce large changes in how much is reflected.

10.2The tank circuit

The simplest matching network, used on our board (Chapter 3), is an inductor L in series with the sensor, together with the parasitic capacitance Cp of the bond pad and wiring in parallel with the sensor. This "tank" behaves like a resonator: near its resonance frequency

\[ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_p}} \approx 205\ \text{MHz} \quad (L = 1.2\ \mu\text{H},\ C_p = 0.5\ \text{pF}), \]

the inductor and capacitor together step the sensor's resistance R down to an effective resistance of

\[ R_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{L}{R\,C_p}. \]

The match is perfect (Reff = Z₀, Γ = 0) when the sensor's resistance equals

\[ R_{\text{match}} = \frac{L}{Z_0\,C_p} = \frac{1.2\ \mu\text{H}}{50\ \Omega \times 0.5\ \text{pF}} = 48\ \text{k}\Omega. \]

This is the single most important formula in reflectometry design: it tells you which sensor resistance the circuit is optimized for. Our sensor, on the flank of its peak, has a resistance of 50 to 100 kΩ, which is close.

The parasitic capacitance is not known precisely before cooldown, and it is the main reason real tanks miss their design. Groups that need control over matching add tunable elements, such as varactor diodes, whose capacitance can be set with a voltage at low temperature [5].

10.3Finding the resonance

The first reflectometry measurement on a cold device is a frequency sweep. A network analyzer, or the readout source and demodulator stepping in frequency, records the reflected amplitude and phase around the expected resonance, first with the sensor pinched off (R → ∞) and then with it conducting. Three things are read off:

  • The resonance frequency. In our device it comes out at 196 MHz instead of the estimated 205 MHz, so the real parasitic capacitance is about 0.55 pF.
  • The depth of the dip when the sensor conducts, which tells you how close to matched it is.
  • The width of the dip, which sets the resonator's bandwidth f₀/QL. With a loaded quality factor of about 20, our tank responds in about 1/(2π × 10 MHz) ≈ 16 ns. That is fast enough never to be the limit; the limit will be noise.

Then the carrier frequency is chosen, usually at or very near f₀, where the response to a change in sensor resistance is largest. Sweeping the sensor plunger SP at that frequency should show the sensor's Coulomb peaks in the reflected signal, now at microsecond speed.

10.4From reflected wave to number: demodulation

The reflected wave comes back up through the cold directional coupler and the HEMT amplifier (Chapter 4) and is demodulated into its two quadratures I and Q (Chapter 5). A change in the sensor's resistance moves the signal point in the IQ plane along some direction set by the circuit and cable delays. Before thresholding, the IQ data are rotated so that this direction lies along one axis, and only that axis is kept. All of the signal is then in one number, and the orthogonal axis, which carries only noise, is discarded. The same rotation is applied to every subsequent measurement [6].

10.5How much power?

More carrier power means a larger reflected signal and a better signal-to-noise ratio, up to a point. The carrier is an oscillating voltage across the sensor, and once its amplitude becomes comparable to the width of the sensor's Coulomb peak, it smears the peak out and heats the reservoirs. The optimum is where the sensor's response per electron, relative to the noise, is largest (Figure 10.4).

Worked numbers: how small is the signal?

At −100 dBm (10⁻¹³ W) in 50 Ω, the carrier amplitude is V = √(2PZ₀) = √(2 × 10⁻¹³ × 50) ≈ 3.2 µV. Small compared with the sensor peak width in bias (hundreds of µV), as it should be.

Suppose one electron changes |Γ| by 0.05. The reflected amplitude then changes by about 0.16 µV.

The noise is set by the system noise temperature, a few kelvin for a good HEMT, more once cable and coupler losses are included. With Tsys = 10 K and an integration time t, the rms noise voltage is roughly √(kBTsysZ₀/(2t)). For t = 2 µs that is √(1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 10 × 50 / 4 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 0.04 µV.

The signal-to-noise ratio is therefore about 4 in 2 µs, and it grows as the square root of the integration time. Every decibel lost between the tank and the HEMT, and every kelvin of amplifier noise, comes straight off this budget.

10.6Signal-to-noise ratio versus integration time

The figure of merit for a charge sensor is how long it must integrate to tell two charge states apart. Prepare the two states (for example, by sitting on either side of a charge transition), record many single measurements of each with integration time t, and histogram them (Figure 10.5). The SNR is the separation of the two peaks divided by their width. For white noise it grows as √t, so a plot of SNR versus t extrapolates to SNR = 1 at the minimum integration time tmin [5].

For Gaussian noise and a threshold halfway between the two peaks, the probability of assigning the wrong charge state in a single shot is

\[ \epsilon = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{\text{SNR}}{2\sqrt{2}}\right), \]

which is 16% at SNR = 2, 1.2% at SNR = 4.5, and 0.13% at SNR = 6. That is why SNR of about 5 to 10 is the usual target for single-shot spin readout (Chapters 16 and 17).

10.7Gate-based sensing: reflectometry without a sensor dot

A sensor dot costs space: its own gates, its own reservoirs, and a position within a dot pitch or two of the qubits. In large arrays this becomes a serious constraint. An alternative is to attach the tank circuit not to a sensor's ohmic contact but to one of the qubit device's own gates. When an electron tunnels between two dots, or between a dot and a reservoir, in response to the small RF voltage on that gate, the gate sees an extra, state-dependent capacitance (the quantum or tunnelling capacitance). That shifts the tank's resonance slightly, which is measured in the reflected phase [5].

This gate-based (dispersive) sensing needs no extra sensor at all, and single-shot spin readout has been demonstrated with it in silicon devices [38, 39, 40, 41]. Its signal is usually weaker than a good sensor dot's, and it only sees charge movement that the gate's RF voltage can drive, but it scales far better. Many groups expect large processors to rely on it.

10.8Reading many sensors at once

Reflectometry has one more advantage: different tanks can be built with different inductors and therefore different resonance frequencies, connected to a single input line and a single output line and amplifier. Each sensor is probed by its own carrier tone and demodulated separately. This frequency multiplexing lets one amplifier chain read several sensors simultaneously; Harvard read four singlet–triplet qubits this way [42]. Our device has one sensor, but the technique becomes essential with more.

When it goes wrong

What you see: the reflected signal barely changes when the sensor is swept through its Coulomb peaks, although the DC current shows the peaks clearly.

Likely causes: the tank is badly mismatched, so the sensor resistance is far from L/(Z₀Cp); the carrier frequency is not at the resonance; the carrier is too weak or far too strong; or the reflected signal is lost through a broken output line or a missing amplifier bias.

What to do: sweep the frequency with the sensor conducting and pinched off. If the resonance barely changes depth between the two, the match is poor. Tune the sensor towards the resistance the tank prefers, if its peaks allow it, or change the inductor in the next cooldown.

Check yourself

1. Your tank uses L = 820 nH and has Cp = 0.6 pF. What is the resonance frequency, and which sensor resistance is matched?

Show answer
f₀ = 1/(2π√(820 nH × 0.6 pF)) ≈ 227 MHz, and Rmatch = L/(Z₀Cp) = 820 nH / (50 Ω × 0.6 pF) ≈ 27 kΩ.

2. A sensor has tmin = 200 ns. How long must you integrate for an assignment error of about 1%?

Show answer
An error of 1% needs SNR ≈ 4.65 (from ε = ½ erfc(SNR/2√2)). Since SNR = √(t/tmin), t = 4.65² × 200 ns ≈ 4.3 µs.

3. Why does increasing the carrier power stop helping beyond a certain point?

Show answer
The carrier is an AC voltage across the sensor. When its amplitude becomes comparable to the width of the sensor's Coulomb peak, it averages the sensor's response over the peak, which flattens the slope that the measurement relies on. It also heats the reservoirs. Beyond that point the signal per electron falls while the noise stays the same.

Part D · Seeing single electrons fast · Chapter 11

The double dot: stability diagrams, the last electron and virtual gates

With a fast sensor, two-dimensional maps of the device's charge states take seconds instead of hours. The map of a double dot, its charge stability diagram, is the most important picture in the field: it shows how many electrons sit in each dot for every pair of gate voltages. This chapter teaches you to read it, uses it to empty both dots down to a single electron each, and introduces virtual gates, which make the map rectangular and the device far easier to control.

11.1Forming the double dot

A double dot needs three tunnel barriers: B1 between the left reservoir and dot 1, B2 between the two dots, and B3 between dot 2 and the right reservoir. The outer barriers B1 and B3 are set so that each dot exchanges electrons with its reservoir easily on the time scale of a map (a few kilohertz or faster). The middle barrier B2 is set lower, so the two dots are distinct but still tunnel-coupled. The plungers P1 and P2 then choose how many electrons each dot holds.

The map is taken by stepping P1 and P2 over a grid while the RF sensor integrates for a few microseconds at each point. With 200 × 200 points at 10 µs each, a complete map takes under a second, so the effect of every other gate can be explored almost interactively. The sensor plunger is compensated throughout (Chapter 9), and the map is usually plotted as the derivative of the sensor signal, which turns each charge transition into a thin line.

11.2Reading the honeycomb

The diagram is made of hexagonal cells, which is why it is often called a honeycomb [43]. Every feature has a meaning:

  • Inside a cell the electron numbers (N₁, N₂) are fixed. Nothing changes as you move around within it, so the sensor signal is flat.
  • The steep lines mark where dot 1's electrochemical potential crosses its reservoir's Fermi level: N₁ changes by one. They are nearly vertical because P1 couples strongly to dot 1, and tilted because P2 couples to dot 1 too. Their slope is −α11/α12, the ratio of the two plungers' lever arms on dot 1.
  • The shallow lines are dot 2's transitions, with slope −α21/α22. They appear stronger in the map because dot 2 is closer to the sensor.
  • The short interdot segments connect the corners of neighbouring cells. Along them, one electron moves between the dots, (1,0) ↔ (0,1) for example. They are the most important lines for spin qubits: Pauli spin blockade readout (Chapter 16) and the exchange interaction (Chapter 24) both happen close to an interdot transition.
  • Triple points at the ends of each interdot segment are where three charge states are degenerate. The length of the interdot segment is set by the mutual charging energy, the extra energy an electron in one dot costs an electron in the other. In our map it corresponds to about 0.9 meV.

The spacing of the lines gives the charging energies. Successive steep lines are separated along P1 by about EC/(eα11), 65 mV here. The ratios of the slopes give the cross-coupling of the plungers, which we will need for virtual gates. Everything in the map is the constant-interaction model of Chapter 7 extended to two dots [43, 1].

11.3Down to the last electron

For single-spin qubits, each dot should hold exactly one electron. The procedure is conceptually simple. Lower both plungers until the map shows a cell with no transitions below or to the left of it, then identify that cell as (0,0) and count up from there.

"No more lines" is a necessary condition for an empty dot, but not a sufficient one, and this is where many hours are lost. As a dot empties, its tunnel barrier to the reservoir becomes thicker and the tunnel rate drops exponentially. When the rate falls below the rate at which the map is swept, the electron no longer leaves when it should, and the transition line first smears, then breaks into a ragged pattern of switching events, then disappears, even though the electron is still there. HRL's first undoped dots showed exactly these regions, where the tunnel rate was slower than the gate modulation [8].

So before declaring (0,0), check that the last lines are sharp, and that they stay where they are when the map is swept more slowly or the outer barrier is opened. Then the absence of further lines means something. Industrial-scale surveys now check this automatically across hundreds of devices on a wafer, measuring where the last electron leaves each dot [31].

When it goes wrong

What you see: near the apparent (0,0) region, the transition lines become blurred or jagged and then fade out, instead of ending cleanly.

Likely cause: the dot–reservoir tunnel rate has become slower than the sweep. The electron is "latched" on or off the dot, missing transitions.

What to do: raise the outer barrier (B1 or B3) to speed up tunnelling, and compensate its effect on the dot with the plunger, or slow the sweep down. If the lines reappear and continue, the dot was not yet empty.

11.4Virtual gates

Look again at Figure 11.1. Because P1 also pulls on dot 2 and P2 on dot 1, every line is tilted, and moving one gate changes both dots. For a double dot this is merely awkward. For the operations ahead it is a real problem: we will need to move dot 1's level without touching dot 2's, change the tunnel barrier between them without moving either level, and pulse along carefully chosen directions in gate space. The standard solution is virtual gates: new control knobs, each a linear combination of physical gates, chosen so that each one acts on only one quantity [44, 1].

The construction follows directly from the lever-arm matrix. To first order, the changes in the two dots' electrochemical potentials are

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \delta\mu_1 \\ \delta\mu_2 \end{pmatrix} = -e \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} \\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \delta V_{P1} \\ \delta V_{P2} \end{pmatrix} = -e\,A\,\delta\mathbf{V}. \]

We want virtual plungers vP1 and vP2 such that vP1 moves only dot 1 (by as much as P1 alone would) and vP2 only dot 2. That means choosing physical voltages

\[ \delta\mathbf{V} = A^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & 0 \\ 0 & \alpha_{22} \end{pmatrix} \delta\mathbf{u} = M\,\delta\mathbf{u}, \]

where δu = (δvP1, δvP2). The software then applies M every time you ask for a virtual-gate change. Only the ratios α12/α11 and α21/α22 are needed, and these are exactly the slopes of the transition lines in the stability diagram.

Worked numbers: our virtual-gate matrix

From the map, dot 1's lines have slope dVP2/dVP1 = −1/0.3 and dot 2's lines −0.3, so α12/α11 = α21/α22 = 0.3. With α11 = α22 = 0.10 eV/V,

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.10 & 0.03 \\ 0.03 & 0.10 \end{pmatrix}\,\text{eV/V},\qquad M = A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 0.10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.10\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.099 & -0.330 \\ -0.330 & 1.099 \end{pmatrix}. \]

A step of +10 mV on vP1 is therefore applied as +11.0 mV on P1 and −3.3 mV on P2. The 3.3 mV taken off P2 cancels P1's pull on dot 2, and the extra 1.0 mV on P1 makes up for the small push the P2 change gives dot 1.

In practice the matrix is larger than 2 × 2. Every gate that matters gets a row and a column: the barriers, whose cross-couplings to the dots are typically 20 to 40% [8], and the sensor plunger, whose compensation becomes one more row. A virtual barrier vB2, for example, raises B2 while lowering P1 and P2 just enough to keep both dots' levels fixed, so that it changes only the tunnel coupling between them. That is the knob used for exchange in Chapter 24 [17, 6].

Three limitations are worth knowing:

  • Linearity is local. Lever arms change as dots grow, shrink and move, so a matrix measured in one region of gate space is only accurate near it. Groups recalibrate the matrix at the operating point they use.
  • It is refined iteratively. Measure the slopes, apply the matrix, map again, and correct the residual tilt. Two or three iterations usually suffice.
  • It is time-consuming for big arrays. With dozens of gates there are hundreds of cross-couplings. Automated extraction from fast maps is an active area [45, 46, 47].

11.5Arrays: adding one dot at a time

In longer arrays, a new problem appears: a dot in the middle has no reservoir of its own, and loading it requires cotunnelling through its neighbours, which becomes impractically slow beyond three or four dots. Transitions go missing and lines from many dots run nearly parallel, so maps become almost impossible to read. QuTech's solution, the "n + 1 method", builds the array one dot at a time from one end. Each new dot is added next to a reservoir, filled, and then isolated by virtual gates that keep the occupations of all previously formed dots fixed. In this way they loaded eight GaAs dots with one electron each [44]. Our two-dot device does not need this, but every larger device does.

11.6Choosing where to operate

For single-spin qubits the natural operating region is the (1,1) cell: one electron in each dot. Readout and initialization will use the neighbourhood of a transition, either a dot–reservoir line (Elzerman readout, Chapter 15) or the (1,1)–(0,2) interdot line (Pauli blockade, Chapter 16). Some groups deliberately work with three electrons in one dot and one in the other, (3,1), because the two inner electrons form a closed shell and the larger dot gives a wider readout window. QuTech's six-qubit device used (3,1)–(4,0) transitions for this reason [6]. For now we park the device in the middle of the (1,1) cell, with both outer barriers set so that each dot can still exchange electrons with its reservoir quickly when needed.

Check yourself

1. In a stability diagram you see one set of lines with slope −4 and another with slope −0.2. Which set belongs to dot 1, and what are the cross-coupling ratios?

Show answer
The steep lines (slope −4) belong to dot 1, since P1 dominates it: α12/α11 = 1/4 = 0.25. The shallow lines (slope −0.2) belong to dot 2: α21/α22 = 0.2.

2. Why are the interdot transition lines the most important lines for spin qubits?

Show answer
Near an interdot transition the two electrons can tunnel between the dots. The singlet–triplet energy structure there allows Pauli spin blockade readout, and the exchange interaction between the two spins, used for two-qubit gates, arises from tunnelling across the same barrier. Both are controlled by the detuning from that line and by the interdot tunnel coupling.

3. Using our matrix M, what physical voltage changes implement a virtual step of +5 mV on vP2 only?

Show answer
δV = M (0, 5 mV): δVP1 = −0.330 × 5 = −1.65 mV and δVP2 = 1.099 × 5 ≈ +5.5 mV.
