Part D · Seeing single electrons fast · Chapter 12

Tunnelling: rates, couplings and spectroscopy

How fast an electron can hop between a dot and its reservoir, and how strongly it is coupled to the neighbouring dot, decide almost everything that comes next. Spin readout needs the dot–reservoir rate in a narrow window. Pauli-blockade readout needs a suitable interdot coupling. The exchange interaction behind two-qubit gates is tunnelling in disguise. This chapter measures and sets these rates, and on the way introduces two powerful tools: the detuning axis and photon-assisted tunnelling.

12.1The detuning axis

Zoom in on one interdot transition of the stability diagram, the one between (1,0) and (0,1). Moving along the transition line changes the total energy of both configurations together. Moving across it changes their energy difference. That difference is the detuning ε, and the direction in gate space that changes ε without changing the total is the detuning axis. With virtual gates it is simply vP2 − vP1, scaled so that ε is in units of energy:

\[ \varepsilon = e\,\alpha\,(\delta v_{P2} - \delta v_{P1}) \quad \text{(for equal lever arms } \alpha\text{)}. \]

Every operation near an interdot transition is described along this axis: initialization, readout, exchange. It is worth setting up a virtual detuning gate in the software, together with its orthogonal partner (both plungers moving together), so that pulses can be programmed directly in ε.

12.2Tunnel coupling and the interdot anticrossing

If the two dots were not coupled at all, the electron would sit in dot 1 for ε < 0 and in dot 2 for ε > 0, with an abrupt switch at ε = 0, smeared only by temperature. With a tunnel coupling tc between them, the two charge states mix near ε = 0 into bonding and antibonding molecular states, separated by

\[ \Omega = \sqrt{\varepsilon^2 + 4t_c^2}. \]

The electron's position, which is what the sensor measures, then changes smoothly across a width set by tc (Figure 12.1). In thermal equilibrium the probability of finding it in dot 2 is [48]

\[ P_2(\varepsilon) = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \frac{\varepsilon}{\Omega}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Omega}{2k_BT_e}\right)\right]. \]

Fitting a sensor trace across the transition with this formula gives tc, as long as tc is not much smaller than kBTe. Then temperature dominates, and the fit only gives an upper bound. Larger couplings also visibly round the corners of the honeycomb cells, and HRL extracted tc from that curvature [8]. For accurate values, especially in the range that matters for qubits, a frequency measurement is better.

12.3Photon-assisted tunnelling

Apply a continuous microwave tone of frequency f to one of the plungers, and sweep the detuning. Wherever the photon energy hf matches the splitting Ω between the bonding and antibonding states, the microwaves drive the electron into the excited charge state, which sits mostly in the "wrong" dot. The sensor sees this as an extra peak (or dip) beside the interdot transition. Repeating at many frequencies traces out the dispersion Ω(ε) directly (Figure 12.2). This is photon-assisted tunnelling (PAT) [49].

PAT is the most precise way to measure the interdot coupling, and it does double duty. The asymptotes of the hyperbola give the lever arm along the detuning axis without any transport measurement. The same technique measures excited-state energies, such as valley splittings, which show up as additional resonance lines. HRL used PAT to measure valley energies of 70 and 14 µeV in two dots of their exchange-only device [50]. It also checks, early on, that microwaves actually reach the gate they are applied to, which matters before you rely on that gate for EDSR (Chapter 18).

12.4Dot–reservoir tunnel rates

The rate Γ at which an electron tunnels between a dot and its reservoir is controlled by the outer barrier, B1 for dot 1 and B3 for dot 2. It depends exponentially on the barrier voltage: HRL found the rate changing as exp(V/12.8 mV), one decade per about 30 mV, and could tune it over nine orders of magnitude with a single gate [8]. Because of this exponential sensitivity, the rate must be measured, not guessed, and it must be measured at the configuration where it will be used: moving a plunger changes the barrier as well.

Three methods cover the whole range:

  1. Smearing of transition lines (slow rates). Apply a square wave of frequency f to the plunger while sweeping across a dot–reservoir transition. If Γ is much larger than f, the electron follows the square wave and the transition appears split into two copies. If Γ is smaller, it cannot follow and the lines blur. The crossover gives Γ to within a factor of a few, which is quick and useful for orientation [8].
  2. Averaged time-resolved response (kilohertz to megahertz). Pulse the dot level from above the Fermi level to below it and back, and record the sensor signal after each edge, averaged over thousands of repetitions. The occupation relaxes exponentially, and fitting gives the loading and unloading rates (Figure 12.3).
  3. Single-shot dwell times (rates below the sensor bandwidth). Park the level at the Fermi level and record the random telegraph signal (Chapter 9). Histograms of the times spent in each state are exponential, with time constants 1/Γin and 1/Γout.

Different stages of the experiment want very different rates, which is why the barriers are re-tuned (or pulsed) between stages:

PurposeRate wantedWhy
Fast charge maps≳ 1 MHzThe electron must follow the gate sweep, otherwise lines smear (Chapter 11).
Elzerman readout≈ 10–100 kHzSlow enough for the sensor to see each event, fast enough to beat spin relaxation (Chapter 15).
Holding a qubit in placeas slow as possibleThe electron must not swap with the reservoir during manipulation.
Isolated operation (no reservoir)≲ 1 Hz, effectively zeroElectrons stay in the array for days, and readout uses Pauli blockade. QuTech kept their six electrons in the array for over a month [6].

12.5Interdot coupling versus barrier

The interdot tunnel coupling, controlled by the middle barrier B2, is just as exponential: HRL measured tc ∝ exp(VX/10.1 mV) for their interdot gate [8]. In our device, tc runs from below 1 µeV ("off") to well over 100 µeV over 60 mV of vB2 (Figure 12.4, right). That range matters for two reasons. For Pauli-blockade readout (Chapter 16), tc must be large enough for the singlet to tunnel quickly into (0,2), typically 10 to 50 µeV. For two-qubit gates, the exchange interaction J ≈ 4tc²/U, with U the charging energy, must be switchable from almost zero to megahertz, which requires exactly this exponential control (Chapter 24). The virtual barrier vB2, which changes tc without moving either dot, is the knob for both.

12.6Pulsed-gate spectroscopy of excited states

One more measurement in the same family finds a dot's excited states without bias, which is useful once transport no longer works. Apply a square wave to the plunger that alternately lifts the dot level above the Fermi level and drops it below. With a small amplitude, only the ground state drops below the Fermi level, and electrons load into it at its tunnel rate. When the amplitude is large enough to pull an excited state below the Fermi level too, a second loading channel opens and the average sensor signal changes. The pulse amplitude at which that happens, times the lever arm, is the excited-state energy. Princeton measured orbital energies of about 3 meV in each of their nine dots this way [7]. The same idea, with spin states instead of orbitals, will be the basis of the spin readout in Chapter 15.

When it goes wrong

What you see: the PAT map shows no resonance, although the sensor clearly sees the interdot transition.

Likely causes: the microwaves are not reaching the gate (a broken or badly attenuated line, a bias tee that blocks high frequencies, a bad bond); the power is far too low; or the tunnel coupling is so large that the gap 2tc/h lies above your frequency range.

What to do: raise the power gradually and look for broadening of the interdot line, which shows that some microwave power arrives. Check the line's transmission at room temperature in the next warm-up. Lower tc with vB2 to bring the gap into range.

Check yourself

1. A PAT hyperbola has its minimum at 6 GHz. What is tc, in µeV and in GHz?

Show answer
2tc/h = 6 GHz, so tc/h = 3 GHz, which is 3 × 4.136 µeV ≈ 12.4 µeV.

2. The dot–reservoir rate is 2 kHz, and you need 30 kHz. With one decade per 30 mV, how much must the barrier change? What else must you adjust?

Show answer
A factor of 15 is log₁₀15 ≈ 1.18 decades, so about 35 mV more on the barrier. The barrier also pulls on the dot level (about 30% of a plunger in our device), so the plunger must be lowered by roughly 10 mV to keep the level in place. With a virtual barrier, this compensation is automatic.

3. Why does the width of the interdot transition stop telling you tc when tc is very small?

Show answer
When 2tc is much smaller than kBTe, the thermal smearing of the occupation is wider than the tunnel-coupling broadening, so the transition width reflects the electron temperature, not tc. PAT, which measures the gap directly as a frequency, remains accurate down to much smaller couplings.
PreviousChapter 11 · The double dot: stability diagrams, the last electron and virtual gatesNextChapter 13 · Pulses: moving gates in nanoseconds

Part D · Seeing single electrons fast · Chapter 13

Pulses: moving gates in nanoseconds

So far every gate voltage has been set by a DC source and left to settle. A qubit experiment instead moves the device through several configurations in every cycle, initialize, manipulate, read, sometimes within a microsecond, and repeats that cycle thousands of times. This chapter is about getting those fast voltage changes onto the gates intact: what the bias tee does to them, how to check that the size you program is the size that arrives, how to find and remove the distortion of fast edges, and how fast pulses also give you a live view of the charge stability diagram.

13.1Why the gates need two paths

The DC lines are heavily filtered to keep the electrons cold and quiet (Chapter 4). Their bandwidth is a few hundred hertz at most, so a voltage step through them takes milliseconds to settle. The fast lines are coaxial cables with attenuators and no low-pass filters, so they pass gigahertz, but they also carry more noise and cannot hold a steady voltage through a long chain of capacitively coupled components. The bias tee on the sample board joins the two (Chapter 3). The DC path sets where the gate sits on average; the coax adds the fast changes on top. Every pulse you program is therefore a deviation from the DC working point, and the gate sees

\[ V_{\text{gate}}(t) = V_{DC} + V_{\text{pulse}}(t) \ast h(t), \]

where h(t) is the response of the fast path: the AWG's own output stage, the attenuators and cables, the bias tee, the bond wire and the gate itself. The rest of this chapter is about the two ends of h(t): what it does on long timescales (the bias tee) and on short ones (everything else).

13.2Slow time scales: the bias tee forgets the average

The capacitor of the bias tee passes changes and blocks steady voltages. Seen from the gate, the pulse path is a high-pass filter with a time constant τ = RC, 2 MΩ × 100 nF = 0.2 s in our board, a cutoff of 0.8 Hz. A pulse much shorter than τ passes almost unchanged. But over many repetitions the capacitor charges up to the average of the pulse sequence, and that average is subtracted from every level (Figure 13.1).

Worked numbers: how much a bias tee moves your levels

A sequence with an average of 7.5 mV shifts every level by 7.5 mV. With a lever arm of 0.10 eV/V, that is 750 µeV, ten times the width of the spin readout window you will set up in Chapter 15 (about 60 µeV). The readout simply stops working, and it stops working gradually over the first second, which makes the cause hard to see.

Within a single long pulse, the level also droops by a fraction t/τ of its amplitude. A 10 mV pulse held for 1 ms droops by 10 mV × 1/200 = 50 µV, or 5 µeV, which is harmless. Held for 50 ms, it droops by 2.5 mV, which is not.

There are three remedies, and most groups use all three:

  • Make every sequence average to zero. Add a compensation segment at the end of the cycle, at the opposite voltage, whose area cancels the rest. Delft's first silicon micromagnet qubit used exactly such a four-stage cycle, initialize, manipulate, read and compensate [9]. Alternatively, shift the whole pulse down by its average, as in Figure 13.1, and move the DC point up by the same amount.
  • Keep pulse lengths much shorter than τ. Long holds belong on the DC path, not in the pulse.
  • Let the bias tee settle. When a sequence starts or changes, the capacitor needs several τ, about a second here, to reach its new state. Running a few hundred cycles before recording any data avoids a slowly drifting start to every measurement.

The same high-pass filtering also limits the fast lines from below: a pulse path with a 0.8 Hz cutoff cannot hold a level for seconds. That is one reason the DC sources are still needed, and why truly static configurations, like the operating point between experiments, always come from them.

13.3Is the pulse the size you programmed?

Between the AWG and the gate are attenuators, usually 20 to 30 dB on the fast lines to keep thermal noise out (Chapter 4), plus the cable losses that grow with frequency. Room-temperature arithmetic gives a first estimate of how much of the programmed amplitude arrives, but the device itself gives the real answer. Apply a square wave to vP1, much slower than the dot–reservoir tunnel rate, and sweep the DC level of vP1 across a charge transition, for a range of programmed amplitudes. The transition then appears twice: once when the DC level reaches it, and once when the top of the pulse does (Figure 13.2).

The slope of the slanted line is the fraction of the programmed amplitude that arrives at the gate, here 0.5, measured with the dot itself, including every attenuator, cable loss and divider. Multiplying by the lever arm converts the AWG's programmed amplitude directly into energy. Do this once for every gate that receives pulses, and repeat it at a few pulse frequencies: if the slope changes with frequency, the fast path's response is not flat, which is the subject of the next section. The same measurement, done with slower and slower square waves, also shows where the bias tee begins to cut in.

13.4Fast time scales: edges that do not stay where you put them

A step programmed on the AWG does not arrive at the gate as a clean step. The coax attenuates high frequencies more than low ones (the skin effect), connectors and bond wires reflect a few percent of the signal, and the bias tee and board components add slow tails of their own. The result is an edge that overshoots, rings, and then creeps toward its final value over hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds (Figure 13.3, left) [25].

Why does a few percent matter? Because so much of what follows depends steeply on gate voltage. The exchange coupling that drives a two-qubit gate changes exponentially with the barrier voltage, by a factor e for every 5 mV in our device (Chapter 24). A 3% error on a 20 mV barrier pulse is 0.6 mV, which changes J by 13% and leaves a conditional phase error of the same relative size after the gate. A singlet–triplet qubit, which is driven entirely by baseband exchange pulses, sees the creeping edge as a chirp in its oscillation frequency (Chapter 27). An Elzerman readout pulse that is still settling in its first microseconds puts the dot's levels slightly in the wrong place just when a spin-up electron is most likely to tunnel out.

The cure is pre-distortion: measure the step response h(t) of each fast line, compute a digital filter that inverts it, and apply that filter to every waveform before it leaves the AWG. Many modern AWGs and control systems include real-time filters for this, typically a few exponential correction stages and a short finite-impulse-response stage for the first nanoseconds.

The step response is best measured where it matters, at the gate. A room-temperature oscilloscope sees the AWG and cables but not the bonds and the sample board. The device itself can act as the oscilloscope: a charge transition is a very sharp voltage reference. Step vP1 by a few millivolts at time zero, and at a variable delay afterwards ask whether the charge transition has been crossed, by measuring the occupation for a range of small DC offsets. The DC offset at which the transition is found at each delay maps out how far the gate is from its target (Figure 13.3, right). The Rochester group developed exactly this, detuning-axis pulsed spectroscopy at the (1,0)–(0,1) transition, to measure each plunger line's response in situ before any spin qubit was tuned up, and corrected the distortions to about a nanosecond with a digital pre-distortion filter [25].

13.5Virtual gates for pulses

The virtual gates of Chapter 11 apply to pulses as well: a pulse on vP1 is sent as a pulse on P1 together with small compensating pulses on P2 and the barriers, so that dot 2 stays put while dot 1 moves. Two details make this work. First, the compensation pulses must arrive at the same moment, so cable delays must be matched, or calibrated and corrected in software, to within a nanosecond or so. Second, the lines must have the same response: if the P1 edge rings and the P2 edge does not, the compensation is right on average and wrong for the first few hundred nanoseconds. Pre-distortion makes all lines look alike, which is another reason to do it before anything that relies on fast virtual-gate pulses, such as exchange gates with compensated barrier pulses (Chapter 24).

13.6Video mode: the charge stability diagram live

With fast lines and fast readout, a charge stability diagram no longer needs a slow raster of DC steps. Instead, a fast sawtooth (or triangle) ramp is applied to vP1 through its bias tee, and a slower stepped ramp to vP2, while the reflectometry signal is digitized continuously. A 100 × 100-pixel map at 2 µs per pixel takes 20 ms, so the diagram can be refreshed many times per second, like a video. Moving a DC knob, a barrier or the sensor plunger, then shows its effect live, and the hours of tuning in Chapter 11 shrink to minutes. Most modern spin-qubit labs tune their devices this way.

Video mode inherits every issue from this chapter. The ramps go through bias tees, so they should average to zero: a symmetric sawtooth centred on the DC point works. The ramp frequency, here 5 kHz for the fast axis, sits far above the bias tee cutoff, so the droop is negligible. Any delay between the ramp and the digitizer shifts the image along the fast axis, and a triangle ramp then shows doubled lines for the up and down halves. The fix is to calibrate the delay until both halves overlap. Finally, the electron has to follow the ramp. Where a dot–reservoir rate falls below the pixel rate, transition lines fade or disappear (Chapter 12), and a missing line in a video-mode map is a statement about tunnel rates, not about charges.

That last point connects to an effect worth knowing by name. When a rate is very slow, the charge state does not change where it would in equilibrium, but stays as it was until a faster path becomes available. The region of the diagram where the "wrong" charge state persists is called a latched region. Latching is a nuisance in fast charge maps, but it is used deliberately for readout: a spin-dependent charge state can be made to latch, which keeps it in place long enough to be measured with a high signal (Chapter 16) [51].

13.7Putting a cycle together

A single-qubit experiment is a repeated cycle of a few stages, each a different gate configuration, with other instruments switched on and off in step. Figure 13.4 shows the cycle for the Elzerman experiments of Part E. In each stage you can already see the logic of the following chapters: the dot is first emptied, then loaded with an electron of the lower-energy spin, then pulled deep into Coulomb blockade so that it cannot exchange electrons with the reservoir while the microwaves rotate its spin, and finally placed where only a spin-up electron can leave.

Getting this cycle right is mostly about timing. All instruments share one 10 MHz reference and one trigger (Chapter 5), but each signal travels a different path. The microwave line has an IQ mixer and different cables, and the readout chain has amplifiers and filters, so their delays relative to the plunger pulse differ by tens of nanoseconds. Each delay is calibrated once, with the device. For the microwave burst, slide it in time across the edge of the manipulation stage and watch where the qubit stops responding (Chapter 18). For the digitizer, look for the plunger edge in the averaged sensor signal. Switching the readout carrier and sensor off during manipulation is not only about timing: both deposit power near the qubit, and QuTech and Princeton both keep them off except during readout [6, 27]. Pulses heat the device too, which shows up as small shifts of the qubit frequency during and after bursts (Chapter 22) [24].

When it goes wrong

What you see: a pulsed experiment works for the first few seconds after you start it and then fades, or a readout point that worked yesterday is off by a few millivolts today, after the sequence was changed.

Likely cause: the sequence's average is not zero, and the bias tee is shifting every level by it. Changing the length of any stage changes the average, and with it the shift.

What to do: compute the average of the sequence and compensate it, automatically, in the software that builds sequences. Check by repeating the pulse-amplitude map of Figure 13.2 with the full sequence running.

What you see: lines in a video-mode map appear doubled, or shifted between the forward and backward sweeps.

Likely cause: a delay between the ramp and the digitizer. What to do: shift the acquisition in time until the two halves overlap, then keep that delay in the configuration.

Check yourself

1. A cycle has stages of 2 ms at +8 mV, 1 µs at +15 mV, 1 ms at +3 mV and 2 ms at 0 mV. What compensation level, held for 1 ms, makes it average to zero?

Show answer
The area is 2 × 8 + 0.001 × 15 + 1 × 3 + 0 = 19.015 mV·ms. A 1 ms compensation stage must cancel it, so its level is −19 mV. That is large, so in practice one would either lengthen the compensation stage (−3.8 mV for 5 ms) or shift all levels down by the average and adjust the DC point.

2. Why is a step response measured with an oscilloscope at room temperature not good enough for pre-distortion?

Show answer
It misses everything between the end of the fridge coax and the gate: the bias tee, the sample board, the bond wires and the gate itself, which contribute some of the slow tails and reflections. The cables also behave differently cold. Measuring with a charge transition includes all of it.

3. In a video-mode map, one transition line is visible at the top of the image but fades out at the bottom. What does that tell you?

Show answer
The tunnel rate for that transition falls along the line, presumably because the gate stepped on the slow axis also closes the barrier. Where it drops below the pixel rate, the electron no longer follows the fast ramp, and the line fades. The charge transition is still there; it is just too slow to see at this speed.

Glossary

Every term defined in the text, in alphabetical order. Click a term to jump to where it is first explained.

addition energy
The difference μ(N+1) − μ(N): the charging energy plus any single-particle level spacing. It sets the height of a Coulomb diamond in bias and its width in gate voltage. (Chapter 8 · Coulomb diamonds, lever arms and electron temperature)
bias tee
A circuit that adds a slowly varying (DC) voltage, delivered through a resistor or inductor, to a fast signal delivered through a capacitor, so both reach the same gate. (Chapter 3 · From chip to sample holder)
charge sensitivity
The smallest charge change detectable with unit signal-to-noise ratio in one second of averaging, δq ≈ e/(SNR·√B), in units of e/√Hz. (Chapter 9 · A charge sensor: counting electrons without current)
charging energy
The electrostatic energy e²/C_Σ needed to add one more electron to a dot, where C_Σ is its total capacitance; several meV in small Si dots. (Chapter 7 · Pinch-offs, barriers and the first dot)
constant-interaction model
A model of a quantum dot in which the Coulomb interaction is captured by a single total capacitance, so adding the N-th electron costs a fixed charging energy plus the single-particle energy of the level it occupies. (Chapter 7 · Pinch-offs, barriers and the first dot)
detuning
The energy difference between two charge configurations of a double dot that differ by one electron moving between the dots, e.g. (1,1) and (0,2); controlled by pulsing the plungers in opposite directions. (Chapter 12 · Tunnelling: rates, couplings and spectroscopy)
electric-dipole spin resonance
Electric-dipole spin resonance: driving spin rotations with an oscillating electric field, which shakes the electron in a magnetic-field gradient (micromagnet) or acts through spin-orbit coupling. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
electron temperature
The temperature that describes the energy distribution (Fermi function) of electrons in the device's reservoirs; usually higher than the fridge temperature because of noise and weak electron–phonon coupling. (Chapter 4 · The fridge as part of the experiment)
gate leak
A steady current from a gate through its oxide into the semiconductor or into another gate; harmless at the pA level, but a sign of damaged or weak oxide when larger. (Chapter 6 · Waking the device up: leakage, turn-on and ohmics)
gate-based (dispersive) sensing
Reflectometry with the resonator attached to one of the device's own gates, detecting the state-dependent capacitance from electron tunnelling instead of using a separate charge sensor. (Chapter 10 · RF reflectometry from the ground up)
honeycomb
The hexagonal pattern of charge states in a double-dot charge stability diagram, bounded by dot–reservoir transition lines and short interdot transition lines. (Chapter 11 · The double dot: stability diagrams, the last electron and virtual gates)
latched
A region of the charge stability diagram where the charge state cannot change on the measurement timescale because the relevant tunnel rate is too slow, so the previous state persists. (Chapter 13 · Pulses: moving gates in nanoseconds)
lever arm
The ratio between a change in a gate voltage and the resulting change in a dot's electrochemical potential, usually quoted in eV/V or µeV/mV. (Chapter 1 · The whole experiment on one page)
minimum integration time
The integration time at which a charge sensor reaches a signal-to-noise ratio of 1 for a single-electron change; a standard figure of merit for fast readout. (Chapter 10 · RF reflectometry from the ground up)
ohmic contacts
A low-resistance electrical contact to the 2D electron gas, made in Si by implanting phosphorus to form a degenerately doped n++ region, and in GaAs by annealing a Ni/Ge/Au alloy. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
overlapping-gate architecture
A gate design in which several metal layers, separated by thin oxide, overlap so that each gate controls one feature (a dot or a barrier) with little cross-talk; introduced for Si by Angus, Zajac and Borselli and co-workers. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
photon-assisted tunnelling
Resonant tunnelling between charge states driven by a microwave photon whose energy matches their splitting; used to measure tunnel couplings, lever arms and excited-state energies. (Chapter 12 · Tunnelling: rates, couplings and spectroscopy)
pinched off
The gate voltage at which the electron gas under a gate is depleted and the channel stops conducting; for a barrier gate, the point below which tunnelling through it becomes negligible. (Chapter 7 · Pinch-offs, barriers and the first dot)
pre-distortion
Shaping the programmed waveform with the inverse of the measured line response, so that the pulse arriving at the gate has the intended shape. (Chapter 13 · Pulses: moving gates in nanoseconds)
random telegraph signal
A signal that switches randomly between two discrete levels, as a sensor does when an electron tunnels on and off a nearby dot. (Chapter 9 · A charge sensor: counting electrons without current)
randomized benchmarking
A protocol that applies long random sequences of gates and measures how fast the survival probability decays, giving an average error per gate that is insensitive to preparation and measurement errors. (Chapter 1 · The whole experiment on one page)
reflection coefficient
Γ = (Z − Z₀)/(Z + Z₀): the complex amplitude ratio of the wave reflected from a load of impedance Z to the wave incident on it through a line of impedance Z₀. (Chapter 10 · RF reflectometry from the ground up)
turn-on
The gate voltage at which a two-dimensional electron gas first forms under a gate in an accumulation-mode device, seen as the onset of current between two ohmic contacts. (Chapter 6 · Waking the device up: leakage, turn-on and ohmics)
undoped
A heterostructure with no intentional dopants; the 2D electron gas exists only where positive gate voltages accumulate it, drawing electrons from implanted ohmic contacts. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
valley splitting
The energy separating the two lowest valley states of an electron in a Si quantum dot, set by the atomic-scale structure of the interface; typically tens to a few hundred µeV in Si/SiGe. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
valleys
Equivalent minima of the conduction band in k-space. Bulk Si has six; tensile strain in a Si/SiGe well lowers the two along the growth direction, and the interface splits those two by the valley splitting. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
virtual gates
Linear combinations of physical gate voltages chosen so that each combination changes only one dot potential or one tunnel barrier, compensating cross-capacitances. (Chapter 11 · The double dot: stability diagrams, the last electron and virtual gates)
visibility
The contrast of a measured oscillation, equal to 1 − α − β for readout error probabilities α and β; also F↑ + F↓ − 1. (Chapter 1 · The whole experiment on one page)
